notes: SCN1A also has gain-of-function disorders. A patient-specific allele must be functionally classified before selecting RNA direction.

disease: SLC6A1-related neurodevelopmental disorder / myoclonic-atonic epilepsy — reviewed loss context
scope: Functional disease-mechanism context based on tested heterozygous loss and missense variants; not a classification of every SLC6A1 allele.
notes: A 213-variant GABA-uptake study supports a haploinsufficiency model and found no dominant-negative effect in its tested subset. Earlier astrocyte/neuron experiments reported possible dominant-negative effects for some variants, including R44Q. The exact allele, cell model, functional wild-type allele and developmental rescue window require separate evidence; gene constraint is not the mechanism evidence.

disease: STXBP1-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy — deletion / reduced-dosage context
scope: Reviewed deletion and transcript-degradation contexts; do not extend this mechanism to all missense alleles.
notes: Isogenic heterozygous human neurons have impaired synaptic transmission. Patient-derived neurons carrying c.429+5G>A show exon-6 skipping, a premature stop, NMD and reduced STXBP1/MUNC18-1. These support dosage loss, not clinical RNA-upregulation efficacy. Protein co-aggregation has been demonstrated for other missense variants; increasing a harmful mutant transcript is not automatically appropriate.

disease: STXBP1-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy — aggregating missense model context
scope: Preclinical functional context for the tested aggregating missense variants; not every STXBP1 allele and not a clinically demonstrated treatment mechanism.
notes: Disease-linked mutant MUNC18-1 co-aggregated wild-type protein in multiple model systems, depleting functional protein beyond hemizygous levels. Chemical chaperone rescue was preclinical. This alternative and the deletion/NMD loss context share disease identifiers, so a disease-only join must remain ambiguous until the selected allele is functionally resolved.

scope: Reviewed heterozygous inactivating/deletion context; does not cover FOXG1 duplication or every DNA-binding missense variant.
notes: Human truncating mutations and a heterozygous mouse model support reduced functional FOXG1. Early postnatal AAV9-FOXG1 rescued selected brain structural deficits in mice; this does not establish a human intervention window, safe overexpression range or reversal of every phenotype. The OMIM identifier is the FOXG1-disorder record, historically named congenital Rett variant.

scope: Reviewed SHANK3 dosage-loss component of Phelan–McDermid syndrome; does not attribute all multigene-deletion phenotypes to SHANK3.
notes: Human isogenic and patient-derived neuronal studies support dosage-dependent functional defects; SHANK3 expression rescued selected cultured-neuron morphology. Mouse overexpression produces abnormal behavior and seizures, so more expression is not presumed safe. Isoform choice, other deleted genes, dosage, cell distribution and developmental timing remain unresolved for therapeutic design; schizophrenia susceptibility is not merged into this context.

scope: Reviewed TCF4 deletion/inactivating context; excludes repeat-mediated corneal disease and does not classify every missense allele.
notes: A human single-gene deletion with cDNA analysis supports haploinsufficiency. Embryonic/neonatal restoration rescued selected mouse outcomes. A December-2025 preprint reports that later juvenile restoration failed most outcomes while improving one cognitive measure; it is not peer-reviewed clinical evidence. Transcript isoforms, functional remaining allele, dose and treatment window require independent resolution.

disease: Pitt–Hopkins syndrome — DNA-binding missense model context
scope: Variant-specific functional hypothesis from homologous substitutions in Drosophila; this does not establish dominant-negative action for every human TCF4 variant.
notes: Some PTHS-linked DNA-binding substitutions introduced into daughterless acted dominantly negatively and failed developmental rescue; other substitutions differed. This model evidence and the human deletion-loss context share a disease ID but concern different variant subsets. Gene-level RNA direction remains unresolved without exact human allele evidence; increasing mutant protein or total dosage cannot be assumed beneficial.

disease: CHD2-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy — reviewed loss context
scope: Reviewed de novo truncating/loss-of-function epilepsy context; missense effects require direct functional work.
notes: Human de novo loss variants and zebrafish knockdown with electrophysiologic seizure-like discharges support dosage loss. A predicted missense consequence or high constraint alone is insufficient to assign this mechanism. No clinical RNA-upregulation benefit, safe dose, delivery, correct isoform or rescue window is established here. OMIM:615369 is currently DEE94; older publications used childhood-onset epileptic encephalopathy terminology.

disease: SCN2A developmental and epileptic encephalopathy — functionally resolved gain subset
scope: Reviewed gain-of-function subset exemplified by R1882Q; this is not a mechanism assignment for all DEE11 alleles.
notes: Patient-derived isogenic cortical-like neurons distinguish R1882Q gain from R853Q loss. Early seizure onset correlates with gain/mixed effects but cannot classify an untested variant. Opposite functional subsets share OMIM:613721, so a disease-only join intentionally remains ambiguous. The adult/neonatal channel splice form and net neuronal effects matter; increasing the mutant gain allele is not presumed appropriate.

disease: SCN2A developmental and epileptic encephalopathy — functionally resolved loss subset
scope: Reviewed loss-of-function subset exemplified by R853Q; not every SCN2A-related epilepsy, autism or ataxia phenotype.
notes: Direct patient-neuron and channel measurements support a loss subset. A larger cohort found loss, gain, mixed and wild-type-like effects, including splice-isoform-dependent classifications. Reduced channel activity is not interchangeable with reduced network excitability. The same disease ID contains opposite variant mechanisms; a useful wild-type allele, mutant-allele effect, isoform and rescue must be established before upregulation is judged.

disease: SCN8A developmental and epileptic encephalopathy — functionally resolved gain subset
scope: Reviewed gain subset, including R850Q and N1768D; does not classify every SCN8A epilepsy allele.
notes: Electrophysiology supports gain properties in specific disease variants. A systematic study shows multiple opposing biophysical changes and exon-5 isoform effects even in established gain variants. Net neuronal action, tissue/developmental isoform and selected allele require direct resolution; raising mutant gain-channel abundance is not presumed appropriate. Separate SCN8A loss phenotypes are not merged into this disease label.

disease: SCN8A cognitive impairment with or without cerebellar ataxia — reviewed loss subset
scope: Reviewed loss subset exemplified by G964R and E1218K; not every SCN8A variant or every related disease.
notes: These two variants prevented sodium currents in transfected cells from patients with intellectual disability without seizures. This differs from the gain-channel DEE context, and loss cannot be inferred merely from annotation. Demonstrating a functional remaining allele, relevant cell activity, dose and rescue is still necessary; these studies do not prove an RNA-upregulation treatment effect.
